items.title: Quantum algorithms for multidimensional partial differential equations
items.subtitle: Quantum linear-algebra methods for scientific PDE workloads
items.summary: Research on quantum methods for solving multidimensional PDEs, including circuit-efficient formulations, practical case studies, and singular-value-based approaches.
overview: This research explores how quantum linear-algebra techniques can be used to formulate and solve multidimensional partial differential equations that arise across scientific and engineering applications.
The work emphasizes practical circuit structure, scalability, and validation across representative PDE families rather than treating the quantum algorithm as an isolated mathematical primitive.

sections.heading: Research direction
paragraphs: The central question is how to map structured PDE problems into quantum computations while keeping the circuit construction efficient enough to study on simulators and available hardware.
Recent work extends this direction toward singular-value decomposition and transformation methods for PDEs in areas such as computational fluid dynamics and nuclear physics.

items.title: Particle Track Reconstruction
items.subtitle: A clean-room C++ tracker measured against mkFit on the same TrackML workload
items.summary: The latest optimization pass raised automatic efficiency from 26.2% to 98.0%, cut fake and duplicate rates to about 4%, and produced a controlled candidate-building benchmark that leads mkFit through eight threads on this CPU.
items.visualAlt: Transverse detector view showing hundreds of measured TrackML particle trajectories radiating from the collision region.
items.visualCaption: Transverse view of 500 charged-particle trajectories from TrackML event000001000. Lines connect measured hit coordinates; the image is generated directly from the benchmark data.
overview: I built this project to treat particle tracking as both an estimation problem and a systems problem. The current engine combines helical EKF reconstruction, structure-of-arrays event storage, automatic seeding, geometry-aware trajectory completion, collaborative hit handling, packed binary input, and interchangeable search strategies.

The latest optimization pass changed the benchmark result substantially. On the same 500-track TrackML subset, the automatic pipeline now reaches 98.0% truth efficiency with a 4.28% fake rate and 4.47% duplicate rate. In a narrower truth-seeded candidate-building comparison, the current core is also faster than mkFit's clone-engine timed section from one through eight threads on this machine. That comparison is deliberately scoped to candidate building; it is not a claim about an entire CMS reconstruction chain.

sections.heading: What I benchmarked
paragraphs: I kept the workload fixed while changing the implementation. The source is TrackML event000001000, reduced to the 500 highest-pT charged particles with pT at least 0.5 GeV, |eta| at most 2.5, and at least four recorded hits. The subset contains 5,605 measured hits.

Two measurements use that same subset. The automatic run starts from hits and lets particle-track-reco find its own seeds. The candidate-building comparison instead supplies the same three truth-derived seed hits per reference track to particle-track-reco and mkFit, removing seed finding from the timing question.

sections.heading: Automatic reconstruction now reaches 98% efficiency
paragraphs: The September 12 baseline made the weak point obvious: automatic seeding recovered only 26.2% of the reference tracks, while 47.9% of reconstructed tracks were fake and 39.4% were duplicates. I used that failure as the optimization target rather than hiding it behind the perfect truth-seeded result.

The current default pipeline now covers 490 of the 500 truth particles during seeding and finishes at 98.0% reconstruction efficiency. The fake rate is 4.28% and the duplicate rate is 4.47%. It does this with 661 generated seeds, 99.37% seed purity, and no truth information supplied to the automatic seeder.

figures.alt: Grouped bar chart showing the improvement in efficiency, fake rate, and duplicate rate from the September 12 automatic reconstruction to the current automatic reconstruction and matched truth seeds.
figures.caption: Same 500 reference tracks in every group. The current automatic pipeline moves from 26.2% to 98.0% efficiency while sharply reducing fake and duplicate tracks.

sections.heading: The full automatic pipeline is faster too
paragraphs: The quality improvement did not come from accepting a large throughput regression. Across seven 100-event repetitions, median automatic-pipeline throughput rises from 235.5k reconstructed tracks per second on one thread to 535.0k on eight threads, while the 98.0% / 4.28% / 4.47% quality result stays unchanged.
The 16-thread measurements were noticeably noisier, so I am not using them for the headline scaling claim. The raw 16-thread runs are still included in the benchmark JSON.

figures.alt: Line chart showing median throughput of the current automatic particle reconstruction pipeline from one through eight threads.
figures.caption: Seven repetitions per thread count, 100 iterations per repetition. The quality metrics are unchanged across the plotted runs.

sections.heading: A controlled candidate-building comparison now favors particle-track-reco
paragraphs: For the mkFit comparison I isolated the stage that can be matched most cleanly. Both programs receive the same 500 three-hit truth seeds on the same Intel Core Ultra 7 265K. particle-track-reco runs its candidate builder with hit sharing, track refinement, and trajectory completion disabled. mkFit uses TrackMLGeom, --seed-input cmssw, --build-ce, one event thread, and its CEMX clone-engine timer.

Using seven 100-event repetitions at each thread count, particle-track-reco reaches median throughputs of 0.762, 1.082, 1.540, and 1.931 million seed-tracks per second at 1, 2, 4, and 8 threads. mkFit reaches 0.234, 0.433, 0.757, and 1.091 million. On this controlled workload that is a 3.25x advantage at one thread, narrowing to 1.77x at eight threads.

figures.alt: Line chart comparing absolute candidate-building throughput for particle-track-reco and the mkFit clone engine at one, two, four, and eight threads.
figures.caption: Candidate-building only. Same 500 truth-seeded TrackML tracks, same CPU, seven 100-event repetitions. This is not a full detector-reconstruction or full CMS-stack comparison.

sections.heading: Truth-seeded reconstruction remains exact on this subset
paragraphs: The faster candidate-building path did not trade away the controlled truth metrics. With the matched three-hit seeds, all 500 reference tracks are recovered with zero fake tracks and zero duplicates in the published comparison runs.

That result matters because it separates two questions that are easy to mix together: whether the builder can extend a good hypothesis correctly, and whether the automatic front end can propose good hypotheses in the first place. The current version is now strong on both for this TrackML subset.

sections.heading: What changed in the implementation
paragraphs: The speedup came from removing overhead around the math rather than weakening the reconstruction. Sparse events now use objective-adaptive collaboration by default, so the engine can skip hit-sharing work when its measured conflict signal does not justify the cost. Dense hit IDs use compact lookup tables and stable counting-order logic instead of general hash routing on the common path.

Track refinement and geometry completion were also reworked to avoid repeated hash-set construction. Immutable TrackML geometry indices are cached between iterations, overlap counting uses compact inverted indices where possible, and trajectory completion can parallelize across tracks. The automatic seeding path was tightened at the same time, which is why the quality and throughput curves moved together instead of trading one for the other.
items: Helical EKF reconstruction with structure-of-arrays storage
Automatic, region, displaced, adaptive, ensemble, and fusion seeding paths
Objective-adaptive collaborative hit handling and compact dense-ID claim routing
Geometry-aware trajectory completion with cached detector-surface indices
Packed .ptrkbin I/O, truth matching, residual/pull validation, and benchmark/parity tooling
Interchangeable EKF, A*, ACO, PSO, simulated-annealing, and Hungarian search backends

sections.heading: Reproducibility and limits
paragraphs: These measurements were regenerated on September 14, 2026 from commit 06a5072 on Jupiter, using a Release build under Ubuntu 24.04 in WSL with GCC 13.3. All 33 repository tests pass on this host, including the LP18 scoreboard test that had previously been timing-sensitive.

The result is intentionally narrower than a claim that this is the fastest tracker in every detector or experiment. It is one public TrackML event subset on one CPU. The mkFit number covers its clone-engine candidate-building timer, and the particle-track-reco comparison is configured to isolate its corresponding candidate-building core. Full detector integration, different occupancies, accelerator backends, and experiment-specific reconstruction chains would require separate validation.
items: Selection: 500 highest-pT charged tracks, pT >= 0.5 GeV, |eta| <= 2.5, at least four hits
Automatic study: seven repetitions, 100 iterations each, 1/2/4/8/16 threads; 1-8 published because 16-thread timings were noisier
Candidate-building study: same 500 truth-derived three-hit seeds for both implementations, seven 100-event repetitions per thread count
Published mkFit comparison: 1, 2, 4, and 8 threads; 16-thread raw measurements retained in the benchmark file
